claim: Consider two binary classifiers evaluated on data sets with the same total size \(N\) and the same number \(P\) of actual positives, and require every cell \(TP,FP,FN,TN\) of each confusion matrix to be strictly positive. Let \(F_1=2TP/(2TP+FP+FN)\) and \(B=(TP/P+TN/(N-P))/2\) be balanced accuracy. No pair of admissible classifiers receives opposite strict rankings from \(F_1\) and \(B\) for \(N\le6\). At \(N=6\), weak-order agreement first fails only because, at \(P=3\), \((TP,FP,FN,TN)=(1,1,2,2)\) and \((2,2,1,1)\) have balanced accuracy \(1/2\) while their \(F_1\) scores are \(2/5\) and \(4/7\). At \(N=7\), strict reversal appears for the first time, and there are exactly three unordered reversing pairs across all admissible prevalences \(P\). For \(P=3\), \((1,1,2,3)\) versus \((2,3,1,1)\) has \(F_1\) scores \(2/5<1/2\) but balanced accuracies \(13/24>11/24\). For \(P=4\), the other two reversing pairs are \((1,1,3,2)\) versus \((2,2,2,1)\), and \((2,1,2,2)\) versus \((3,2,1,1)\). Thus controlling both sample size and prevalence does not align the metrics: the smallest strictly positive confusion-matrix sample where they prefer opposite classifiers has seven observations. Common positive scaling preserves both scores, so the \(P=3\) witness recurs at totals \(7q\) for every positive integer \(q\).
integrity: For fixed prevalence each admissible matrix is parameterized by exact integer true-positive and false-positive counts. The package exhaustively compares every pair through the sharp total with exact rational arithmetic and separately verifies the first weak tie and first strict reversal layer.
scientific_limitations: The theorem concerns binary classifiers compared at common sample size and common prevalence with all four confusion-matrix cells strictly positive. It is an exact finite-grid ordering result, not a statement about inferential reliability or uncertainty of estimated performance.
title: Seven cases are the sharp fixed-prevalence F1–balanced-accuracy strict-reversal boundary
